attributes.title: Level 4

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add [connect (tilemap 1) and (tilemap2) by (Door1)] and [set tilemap to] blocks to the [on start] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What type of tilemap is (tilemap1)? What type of tilemap is (tilemap2)?

❓ What do you think connecting (tilemap1) and (tilemap2) will be used for in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡In this project, (tilemap1) is a top-down tilemap and (tilemap2) is a 2D platformer. By connecting the two tilemaps, the Player sprite will be able to move between them through the use of a door tile, coded in later steps.

💡 If the ninja is having trouble adding the tilemap utility extension, guide them through the process. Click and select Extensions, then scroll down to search for the arcade-tile-util extension (shown below) to add it to the code block menu.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by setting up the tilemaps! Explore the two tilemap designs and notice that one has a top down orientation, and the other is a 2D platformer.


Add the tilemap extension to the menu by clicking then selecting Extensions. Scroll down then select the arcade-tile-util extension to add it to the project.


Open Tile Util, then drag a [connect (tilemap 1) and (tilemap2) by (Door1)] block into the [on start] container, under the 2 [set variable to (tilemap)] blocks.


Add a [set tilemap to] block underneath, then drag in a (tilemap1) block as the value.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you call the switchTilemap function in the [on start] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it important to set the Player sprite’s movement differently on a top-down tilemap versus a 2D platformer? 

❓ How might the (current tilemap) block be useful? What does it check for?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that the two different types of tilemaps give the user a different perspective. In a top down tilemap, the user looks onto the project from up above, whereas in a platformer, the user’s perspective is from the side. Consequently, the Player sprite’s movement needs to be programmed differently to reflect these perspectives.
steps.instructions:
Set the Player sprite's movement for the top down tilemap!


Tilemap1 is a top down tilemap, so the Player sprite will be able to move in all 4 directions but will not be able to jump. 


Create a function named switchTilemap. Drag an [if then] conditional inside the function container. Replace <true> with a <0=0> comparison block.


Open Tile Util then place a (current tilemap) block in the left parameter and a (tilemap1) block in the right parameter. Inside the conditional, add a [set sprite [x]] block. Select the Player sprite’s name, [ay (acceleration y)], and leave the value as “0.”


Drag a [move sprite with buttons] block into the conditional opening. Then, add a [place sprite on top of location] block and select the Player sprite’s name.


Call the function in the [on start] container.


Click ▶ to move the Player sprite around the first tilemap in different directions.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you change the vy value in the [move sprite with buttons] block, so the Player sprite may only move left or right when (tilemap2) is the current tilemap?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What is different about the Player sprite’s acceleration and velocity on a platformer tilemap, compared to a top down tilemap? 

❓ What else might happen differently, depending on which tilemap the Player sprite is on?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that they need to code the Player sprite to be able to jump on top of platforms and simulate gravity to fall to the ground in a platformer tilemap, whereas in a top down tilemap, the Player sprite is able to move in all four directions without gravity.
steps.instructions:
Set the Player sprite's movement for the 2D platformer tilemap!


Tilemap2 is a 2D platformer tilemap, so the Player sprite should only be able to move left and right and be able to jump!


Click + in the [if then] conditional 2 times then duplicate the <0=0> comparison block and place it in the <true> value in the [else if] opening. Select (tilemap2) as the right parameter. Click (-) to delete the last [else] opening.


Duplicate all of the blocks from the first opening of the [if then] conditional, but change the [ay] value to 500. In the [move sprite with buttons] block, change the vy value to 0 so the Player sprite can only move left or right. In the [place sprite on top of location] block, update the coordinates to (2, 6).

steps.hints: ❓Did you create a new variable called spriteJump and use it to change when the Player sprite can jump?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why do you think it’s useful to use a variable and a Boolean to set when the Player sprite is able to jump?

❓How does the Player sprite’s velocity y change when they can and cannot jump?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Using a variable and a Boolean can help organize code and program something to happen in a different container. The Player sprite’s velocity y changes to 0 when spriteJump is false so that it is unable to leave the tilemap ground.
steps.instructions:
Set the condition for when the Player sprite can jump! 


Create a new variable called spriteJump, then set it to <false> for tilemap1 and <true> for tilemap2 inside the switchTilemap function’s conditional.


Drag out an <and> Boolean, then place the existing <is sprite hitting wall> value block inside [on [A] button pressed] container in the right parameter. Drag out another <0=0> block and place it in the left parameter. Use a (spriteJump) variable and a <true> Boolean to check if spriteJump is true and the Player sprite is standing on a tilemap wall.


Click + to create an [else] opening. Use a [set sprite [velocity y] to] block in the conditional to set vy to 0 when spriteJump is false or the Player sprite is not standing on a tilemap wall.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add a [load tilemap connected by (Door1)] block and a [call switchTilemap] into the [on sprite overlaps tile] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps the door tile?

 ❓ How are the [connect (tilemap) and (tilemap) by (Door1)] and [load tilemap connected by (Door1)] blocks linked?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The [connect (tilemap) and (tilemap) by (Door1)] block sets the connection between (tilemap1) and (tilemap2). By placing the [load tilemap connected by (Door1)] block in the [on sprite overlaps tile] container, the project is drawing on the previous block when looking for the tilemap connected by (Door1). 

💡Prompt the ninja to reflect on if there have been any previous projects in which having a door tile to connect and switch between tilemaps may have been useful, and how this might be used in future projects.
steps.instructions:
Load the new tilemap with a door tile overlap! 


Open Tile Util and drag a [load tilemap connected by (Door1)] block into the [on sprite overlaps tile] container. Then, add a [call switchTilemap] block into the container.


Set the background color for the 2D tilemap by dragging a [set background color] block into the [else if] opening of the conditional inside the switchTilemap function. 


Click ▶ then move the Player Sprite to the door tile to see the tilemap switch and the Player sprite’s movement change!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an [on each tile create sprite with image and kind] block and a [cover all tiles with tile] block in the [on tilemap loaded] container to create an Item sprite at each Item 1  tile?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the [on tilemap loaded] container work? How does it know when to run?

❓ How is the [on each tile create sprite with image and kind] block similar to how you’ve used a [for element] loop to place sprites?

❓ Why might you use a [cover all tiles with tile] block instead of a [set tile at location] block?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The [on tilemap loaded] container runs code whenever a new tilemap is loaded. 

💡 The [for element] loop has been used previously to spawn tiles to place sprites on. The placeholder tiles and the [on each tile create sprite with image and kind] block work very similarly in this project, it just requires fewer blocks.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the [cover all tiles with tile] block only provides a temporary cover. That means that it will allow items to reappear if a sprite leaves and then later returns to a tilemap. This is not the same when the [replace all tiles with tile] block is used.
steps.instructions:
Place Items on the tilemap placeholders!


Open Tile Util and drag out an [on tilemap loaded] container. Drag an [on each tile create sprite with image and kind] block into the container. Select the Item 1 tile and Item sprite kind. Use the image from the potion sprite’s [set sprite to] block from the [on start] as the sprite image, then delete the empty [set sprite to] block.


Add a [cover all tiles with tile] block to cover all Item 1 tiles with purple dungeon tiles after the sprite has been created. 


Now, the Item1 placeholder tiles in the top down tilemap will be replaced by the potion Item sprites.


Click ▶ to see the Item sprites appear on the top down tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an [on each tile create sprite with image and kind] block and a [cover all tiles with tile] block in the [on tilemap loaded] container to create an Enemy sprite at each NPC 1  tile?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might it be useful to use different types of placeholder tiles to create sprites of different kinds?

❓ What appears on the platformer tilemap now?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide the ninja to open the tilemap editor and notice that a new category of tiles, “TileUtil”, has been added in the drop down menu. These tiles can act as placeholders and can be used to signal locations where something else will happen (e.g. a sprite will be created, an obstacle might be placed, etc.). 

💡Within the TileUtil tile category, there are several tiles with different terms (such as item, NPC (non-player character), and door). Each of these unique terms can be used to make clear what should happen on those tiles.
steps.instructions:
Place Enemies on the placeholder tiles!


Duplicate the [on each tile create sprite with image and kind] block and place it underneath the [cover all tiles with tile] block. Select the NPC 1 tile and Enemy sprite kind; in game design, NPC stands for non-player character. Use the image from the dinosaur sprite’s [set sprite to] block from [on start] as the sprite image, then delete the [set sprite to] block.


Duplicate the [cover all tiles with tile] block, place it underneath the [on each tile create sprite of kind] block, and set it to cover all NPC 1 tiles with a tile that matches the background color selected. 


Drag out an [on created sprite of kind] container and select Enemy in the dropdown. Add an [animate frames] block and select the dinosaur sprite’s animated image from the Gallery. 


Now, dinosaur Enemy sprites will appear on all of the NPC 1 placeholder tiles in the platformer tilemap.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprites appear on the platformer tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use [destroy all sprites of kind] blocks to destroy the Item and Enemy sprites so they do not appear on the wrong tilemap?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓How is the [destroy all sprites of kind] block similar and different to the [destroy sprite] block? 

❓ What else might be changed when the tilemap switches?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The [destroy all sprites of kind] block causes all sprites of a certain kind to be destroyed, whereas the [destroy sprite] block only causes a single sprite to be destroyed.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The Item and Enemy Sprites don’t disappear when the Player sprite moves to a different tilemap. 


Open Sprites and drag a [destroy all sprites of kind] block into the switchTilemap function’s conditional so that all Enemy sprites are destroyed when the tilemap is set to (tilemap1).


Duplicate the [destroy all sprites of kind] block and place it into the [else if] opening, so that all Item sprites are destroyed when the tilemap is set to (tilemap2).


Click ▶ to see the Item and Enemy sprites disappear when the tilemap switches.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an [if then] conditional to check if the (current tilemap) is set to (tilemap2) for the projectile to work?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What condition(s) needs to be true in order for the Player sprite to be able to send a projectile?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk the ninja through the logic in the [on [B] button pressed] container. If the (current tilemap) is set to (tilemap2), which is a 2D platformer, then the conditional checks if the (magicLevel) is greater than or equal to 1, meaning the Player sprite has collected enough Item sprites. If so, a projectile will be sent from the Player sprite and a (magicLevel) point will be lost. Else, the Player sprite will be told to go back and collect more Item sprites.
steps.instructions:
Set the projectiles to only work in the Platformer tilemap. 


Drag out an <and> Boolean, then place the existing <magicLevel >= 1> value block inside [on [B] button pressed] container in the right parameter. Drag out another <0=0> block and place it in the left parameter. 


Open Tile Util and drag a (current tilemap) block into the left parameter with a (tilemap2) block as the right parameter. Now, the projectile code will only work if the Player sprite is in the Platformer tilemap.


Click ▶ to see that the Player sprite can only launch projectiles while it’s on a platformer tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag (otherSprite) into the (tilemap location of (sprite)) block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it important to also set a blank tile even after an Enemy sprite has been destroyed? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If a blank tile is not set to replace the placeholder tile when an Enemy sprite has been destroyed, the Enemy sprite will be reset the next time that the Player sprite returns to the platformer tilemap, because the Enemy sprite is set in the [on each tile create sprite with image and kind] block.
steps.instructions:
Remove the placeholder tile when an Enemy sprite has been destroyed.


Drag a [set tile at location] block into the [on (Projectile) overlaps (Enemy)] container, above the [if then] conditional, Leave it set to a blank default tile. Open Scene and drag a (tilemap location of (sprite)) block into the location parameter. Replace (mySprite) by dragging (otherSprite) into the parameter.


Click ▶ to see that the Enemy sprites do not reappear after they are destroyed by a projectile, even when the Player sprite leaves then returns to the tilemap.

    otherSprite.destroy()
    magicLevel += 1
    playerSprite.sayText(magicLevel, 500, false)
})

        magicLevel += -1
    } else {
        game.showLongText("Go back to the other room to collect more potion!", DialogLayout.Bottom)
    }
})
controller.A.onEvent(ControllerButtonEvent.Pressed, function () {
    if (playerSprite.isHittingTile(CollisionDirection.Bottom)) {
        playerSprite.vy = -250
    }
})
scene.onOverlapTile(SpriteKind.Player, assets.tile`tile2`, function (sprite, location) {
	
})
sprites.onOverlap(SpriteKind.Projectile, SpriteKind.Enemy, function (sprite, otherSprite) {
    sprite.destroy()
    otherSprite.destroy()
    if (sprites.allOfKind(SpriteKind.Enemy).length == 0) {
        game.gameOver(true)
    }
})

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses tilemap extension blocks to switch between a top down tilemap and a 2D Platformer tilemap.

validationItems.text: Connect tilemap1 and tilemap2, and set the current tilemap to tilemap1.
Create a function to set the Player sprite’s movement for both tilemap1 and tilemap2.
Set the condition for when the Player sprite can jump.
Load the connected tilemap when the Player sprite overlaps a specific tile.
Place Item and Enemy sprites on tilemap placeholders.
Destroy Item and Enemy sprites when the tilemap changes.
Set projectiles to work only in tilemap2.
Remove the placeholder tile when Enemy sprites are destroyed.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 4 of Green Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about tilemap location and extension blocks. These blocks can connect different tilemaps more easily and cause different things to happen based on a specific location or tile. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 4:

badges.title: Charting a Course
badges.description: Use the tilemap extension in MakeCode to extend the possibilities in a tilemap project.

badges.title: Neighbors
badges.description: Find the tilemap location next to a specific tile or sprite.

badges.title: GPS
badges.description: Find the exact tile location of a sprite on a tilemap.

badges.title: Ducks in a Row (Or Column)
badges.description: Find the row or column value of a specific location on a tilemap.

badges.title: Atlas
badges.description: Link two different tilemaps together in a project.

badges.title: Area Rug
badges.description: Temporarily cover all tiles of a specific kind on a tilemap.
